# Print-on-Demand Service Compatibility Critique — holiday-card

*Reviewer: Print-on-Demand Service Vetter, 10+ years getting files accepted at MOO, Vistaprint, Catprint, Printful, Mpix, Smartpress.*
*Sample file: `/tmp/pod_test.pdf` (1.6 KB), generated by `holiday-card create christmas-classic`.*

---

## Verdict in one sentence

**Holiday-card produces a perfectly fine *home-printer* PDF, but the output is rejectable-on-arrival at every major print-on-demand service I've worked with — wrong trim size, no bleed, no safe area, RGB-only with no ICC profile, no PDF/X conformance, and an imposition layout that POD pre-press systems explicitly tell you not to send.**

If a customer takes `pod_test.pdf` and tries to upload it to MOO, Vistaprint, Catprint, Printful, or Smartpress today, the order will either be hard-rejected at the preflight step, soft-warned ("we proceeded but cannot guarantee result"), or silently disasterized at the trimmer. None of those are acceptable for a paid greeting card.

---

## What I actually saw in the file

```
File:        /tmp/pod_test.pdf  (1,628 bytes)
PDF version: 1.3
Producer:    ReportLab PDF Library (opensource)
Pages:       1
MediaBox:    612 x 792 pts  (8.5" x 11", US Letter)
TrimBox:     612 x 792 pts  (== MediaBox  → no trim defined)
BleedBox:    612 x 792 pts  (== MediaBox  → no bleed)
CropBox:     612 x 792 pts
OutputIntents: NONE         (not PDF/X-anything)
Color ops:   8 rg/RG (RGB), 0 k/K (CMYK)
Resources:   /Font, /ProcSet only — no embedded ICC, no images this run
Imposition:  4 panels packed on a single 8.5x11 sheet with a dashed fold line
             at y=396pts (the literal trim line is rendered in the artwork)
```

That last point is critical and I'll return to it: a fold-line crop-mark is being **drawn into the content stream as a dashed grey rule**, not declared as page metadata. POD preflight will treat it as artwork and may keep it, leaving a dashed line through the finished card.

---

## What happens if a user uploads this to MOO / Vistaprint / Catprint / Printful / Smartpress

### MOO (postcards / Greeting Cards / notecards)
- **Hard reject at preflight.** MOO accepts only PDFs sized to one of their named products (A6, A5, Square, etc.) plus exactly 2mm (~0.079") bleed on each side. An 8.5×11 file does not match *any* MOO product. The MOO uploader will pop a "this file doesn't match the dimensions for the product you've selected" error and refuse to proceed.
- Even if you forced it past dimension check (you can't), MOO requires CMYK or it converts your RGB on its end — and then their FAQ explicitly says "colour shifts in conversion are not eligible for reprint." This file is RGB.

### Vistaprint (5×7 Greeting Cards, folded)
- Vistaprint's folded greeting card template is a single PDF *per side* (outside spread + inside spread), each at 10.25×7.25" finished spread with 0.125" bleed all around → trim 10×7. Or you upload via their online editor with images per panel.
- Holiday-card's output is one combined sheet, 8.5×11, half-folded to 5.5×8.5. Vistaprint will: (a) flag dimension mismatch, (b) warn no bleed, (c) warn no CMYK, (d) warn text is within the 0.25" cut zone. Order can be force-submitted but lands in their "low quality file" queue and tends to come back with white slivers and shifted reds.

### Catprint (popular Etsy/indie fulfillment for stationery)
- Catprint accepts PDF, PNG, AI, and PSD, but their stationery products have specific trim sizes (A2 4.25×5.5, A6 4.5×6.25, A7 5×7) **with 0.125" bleed.** They have a "vector accepted" workflow which is the *one* place this project's `--format svg` could shine — but the SVG is also sized for the letter sheet, not a Catprint trim spec. So same answer: rejected for size mismatch.

### Printful (4.25×5.5 folded greeting card)
- Printful's spec: 4.25×5.5 finished, 4.5×5.75 with bleed, 300 DPI, RGB sRGB *accepted* (they're one of the few). They want a single PDF/PNG/JPG **per side**, not an imposed sheet. Holiday-card's combined-sheet output cannot be uploaded — Printful's UI has explicit "Front" / "Inside" / "Back" upload slots and they want you to drop one image into each.

### Mpix (folded photo cards)
- Mpix is photo-card focused (5×7 flat or folded). Accepts JPG/PNG/PDF at exact pixel dimensions per product (e.g., 1500×2100 for 5×7 at 300 DPI). Imposed PDF sheet → reject.

### Smartpress (professional shop)
- Smartpress is the strictest. Their preflight requires **PDF/X-1a or PDF/X-4**, embedded ICC profile (they default to GRACoL 2013 CRPC6), CMYK process or named spots, all fonts embedded, 0.125" bleed and 0.125" safety. This file is none of those. It will be rejected before a human sees it.

---

## The format / trim-size mismatch (the load-bearing problem)

Every constant in `src/holiday_card/utils/measurements.py` is hard-coded around US Letter:

```python
PAGE_WIDTH  = 8.5
PAGE_HEIGHT = 11.0
HALF_FOLD_WIDTH  = PAGE_HEIGHT / 2  # 5.5"
HALF_FOLD_HEIGHT = PAGE_WIDTH       # 8.5"
```

So a "half-fold" card is **5.5 × 8.5 finished**. Compare to what POD services actually sell:

| Service        | Folded greeting card finished sizes              |
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| MOO            | A6 4.13×5.83, A5 5.83×8.27, Square 5.5×5.5       |
| Vistaprint     | 5×7, 4.5×6.25, square 5×5                        |
| Catprint       | A2 4.25×5.5, A6 4.5×6.25, A7 5×7                 |
| Printful       | 4.25×5.5                                         |
| Mpix           | 5×7, 4×8, 5×5                                    |
| Smartpress     | Custom — but you set up the doc to spec          |

**5.5 × 8.5 is not on any of those lists.** Letter half-fold is a Microsoft Word / Hallmark-template-from-1998 size, not a commercial stationery trim. It exists *only* because 8.5×11 is the cheapest thing to feed into a desktop laser printer. The whole geometry of this app is implicitly "you have an HP at home, fold it yourself, hand it to grandma."

That is a 100% legitimate use case — but it is mutually exclusive with "I want to order 50 of these for my friends from MOO."

## Per-service spec table

| Service     | Trim (finished folded) | Bleed   | Safe area | Color           | File format               | Compat today | What's missing                                   |
|-------------|------------------------|---------|-----------|-----------------|---------------------------|--------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| MOO         | A6 4.13×5.83           | 2 mm    | 4 mm      | CMYK preferred  | PDF (X-1a/X-3 preferred)  | 0%           | Trim, bleed, CMYK, PDF/X, per-panel files        |
| Vistaprint  | 5×7                    | 0.125"  | 0.125"    | CMYK preferred  | PDF, JPG, PNG             | 0%           | Trim, bleed, per-side spreads, CMYK              |
| Catprint    | 4.25×5.5 / 4.5×6.25    | 0.125"  | 0.125"    | CMYK preferred  | PDF, PNG, AI, PSD         | 0% PDF / 5% SVG (close but wrong size) | Trim, bleed, per-side, CMYK |
| Printful    | 4.25×5.5               | 0.125"  | 0.125"    | sRGB OK         | PDF, JPG, PNG (per side)  | 0%           | Trim, bleed, per-panel exports                   |
| Mpix        | 5×7 / 4×8              | 0.125"  | 0.125"    | sRGB OK         | JPG/PNG at exact pixels   | 0%           | Trim, bleed, raster export at fixed pixel dims   |
| Smartpress  | Custom                 | 0.125"  | 0.125"    | CMYK + ICC      | PDF/X-1a or PDF/X-4 only  | 0%           | PDF/X conformance, ICC, CMYK, bleed, font embed  |

Every cell that says 0% is a hard fail at upload, not a polish issue.

---

## What needs to change in the IR / compiler / CLI

These are concrete, in roughly the order I'd ship them:

1. **Decouple "page" from "card."** Today `measurements.py` collapses sheet size, panel size, and finished-card size into one set of letter constants. Split into `Sheet` (what the printer sees), `Trim` (what the customer holds), and `Bleed` / `Safe`. Half-fold on letter becomes one of *many* `(Sheet, Trim, Bleed, Safe)` configurations, not the only one.

2. **Add a `--export-for` (a.k.a. `--print-target`) flag on `create`.** Plumb a `PrintTarget` enum: `home`, `moo-a6`, `moo-square`, `vistaprint-5x7`, `catprint-a2`, `printful-folded`, `mpix-5x7`, `smartpress-generic`. This is the single most valuable change. With it, a customer's workflow becomes:

   ```
   holiday-card create christmas-classic --export-for moo-a6 -o card.pdf
   ```

   …and the same template renders to a different sheet, with the right trim, the right bleed, and exported the way that service expects (single sheet vs per-panel files).

3. **Bleed-aware coordinates.** Templates currently position everything in inches inside a 5.5×8.5 panel with no notion of bleed. A `bleed` field on `Panel` and a compiler pass that auto-extends background fills past the trim line by `bleed_size` would do it. Today, the front-panel red fill in `christmas-classic` stops *exactly* at the trim line (x=4.25 to x=8.5), so any tiny shift on a guillotine produces a white sliver on three edges. This is the textbook bleed bug.

4. **A real safe-area validator.** `validate_within_panel()` exists, but it uses `SAFE_MARGIN = 0.25"` as the *only* concept. Per service, safe area is different from bleed and from trim. The validator should warn (not just refuse) when a text element falls outside the safe zone for the chosen `--export-for` target.

5. **CMYK paint type + ICC.** ReportLab supports `setFillColorCMYK` and you can register an ICC OutputIntent. Today the renderer hard-codes `setFillColorRGB` (lines 266, 280, 295 of `reportlab_backend.py`). Add a `ColorSpace` parameter on the renderer; when target == any pro POD, paint in CMYK and embed GRACoL 2013 CRPC6 (free from Adobe / IDEAlliance) as the OutputIntent.

6. **PDF/X-1a or PDF/X-4 output mode.** ReportLab can almost get there but needs explicit work: PDF version ≥ 1.4, OutputIntent dictionary, no transparency in X-1a, all fonts subset-embedded, MediaBox/TrimBox/BleedBox set distinctly. None of this exists today (PDF version is 1.3, all three boxes are identical). The package `pdfx` or a post-process via `ghostscript -dPDFX` is the pragmatic path.

7. **Per-panel exporter for "imposition-by-service" workflows.** For Printful, MOO, Vistaprint et al. who do their own imposition, the compiler already has the IR — just emit one PDF per `Panel` instead of imposing them onto a sheet. Add `holiday-card export-panels christmas-classic --target printful -o ./out/` that produces `front.pdf`, `inside.pdf`, `back.pdf` already trimmed-flat with bleed.

8. **Stop drawing the fold line as content.** The fold-line dashed rule at y=396pts is rendered into the PDF stream. For home printing it's a helpful guide. For POD it's content that will show on the finished card. Move it behind a `--with-fold-marks` flag, default off when `--export-for` is anything other than `home`.

9. **DPI declaration / raster export at fixed pixel dimensions for Mpix-style services.** PNG renderer already has a `--dpi` flag — extend the same target system so `--export-for mpix-5x7` produces a 1500×2100 PNG with the safe-area validator turned on.

---

## The architectural question

> Should holiday-card be the *imposition tool*, or just produce *trimmed-flat panel assets* and let the service do imposition?

This is the fork in the road. Right now it's an imposition tool that imposes for one specific output (home laser, letter, half-fold). Every POD service in my list *also* does imposition — and they want unimposed input. So the project is currently solving a problem the print services already solve, in a way they reject.

My recommendation: **make it both, gated by `--export-for`**.

- `--export-for home` (default): keep current behavior. Impose front/back/inside on a single sheet, draw the fold line, hand to the user's printer. This is what home users want and the project already nails it.
- `--export-for <pod>`: treat the card as a logical 4-panel object, emit *trimmed-flat per-panel files with bleed and CMYK* exactly the way that POD wants them. Skip the imposition step entirely.

Same templates. Same IR. Different backend output. The IR is already the right abstraction for this — `compile_card → list[RenderCommand]` is service-agnostic; what changes is the page setup and the file-packaging at the end.

---

## What's surprisingly good

A few things this project gets *right* that I'd usually be telling someone to add:

- **A real intermediate representation.** `compile_card` produces a list of `RenderCommand` objects that drive multiple backends (PDF, SVG, PNG). That's exactly the architecture you need to add a "POD-pro" backend without rewriting everything. This is rarer than you'd think in print tooling.
- **SVG output.** Catprint's "vector accepted" path and any future Risograph / letterpress shop wants SVG. The SVG backend already exists. It just needs a proper trim/bleed/document-size pass.
- **Inches as the source-of-truth unit.** `inches_to_points()` everywhere; no pixel sloppiness. This is what every print engineer asks for and it's already there.
- **TTF/OTF font embedding** (per CLAUDE.md). PDF/X requires all fonts embedded. The font-loading path already does the hard part.
- **Validators per panel.** `validate_within_panel` already exists. It's the right place to bolt a real safe-area check.
- **Clean YAML templates.** Easy to author per-service variants without code changes — the template system is already factored to support it.

---

## The leapfrog opportunity

**Ship `--export-for moo-a6` (or pick any one POD service) end-to-end as a single, complete, opinionated path: A6 trim, 0.125" bleed, CMYK, embedded GRACoL ICC, PDF/X-1a, per-panel files, MOO's exact dimension tolerance, validated to pass MOO preflight on the first upload.**

That's the leapfrog. There is *no* open-source greeting-card generator today that produces a file you can drop into MOO and have it accepted without preflight warnings. Hallmark-style desktop tools cost $80 and don't do CMYK. Affinity / Adobe require you to design the card from scratch. If holiday-card becomes "the tool that makes MOO-ready holiday cards from a YAML template," it owns a real niche — and the home-printing path doesn't have to change at all to get there.

The 80/20 cut: pick MOO (because A6 is the most common indie greeting card spec, and MOO's preflight is well-documented), nail it, then template-clone the work for Catprint and Vistaprint. After three services it's basically a configuration problem, and the project becomes the only OSS option for "design a card once, print it at home OR ship it through any POD service."

That, not more decorative elements or more occasions, is what would put this project on Hacker News.
